A8: Thank you very much for the helpful suggestion! We agree that the confinement of H and Cl
2 2
generation to the terminal electrodes (Pt cathode for HER and graphite anode for CER, as shown in
Fig. 1b) could appear limiting at first glance. However, this design choice is primarily driven by safety
considerations: by isolating the HER and CER at opposite ends of the serially connected units, we can
prevent the mixing of H and Cl gases, reducing risks that are prevalent in conventional chlor-alkali
2 2
processes where gases are produced in shared compartments.
Our system can be adapted for higher scalability. As illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 42, the
design allows for straightforward adaptations through serial and parallel connection to adjust
production rates.
Increasing the number of serially connected units (e.g., from 18 to more, as depicted in
Supplementary Fig. 42a) raises the overall electrochemical reaction voltage. This enhancement in
voltage accelerates the chlorine evolution reaction (CER) kinetics, thereby boosting Cl production
2
rates. For instance, our experiments with varying unit numbers (Supplementary Fig. 29) showed that
stacking more units (up to 18 in the integrated device, Supplementary Fig. 30) linearly increases the
open-circuit voltage (Fig. 5e), enabling higher throughput while keeping the terminal electrodes fixed
for gas isolation.Caution is needed to avoid excessively high voltages, which may trigger competing
oxygen evolution reactions and lower Faraday efficiency.
To amplify the reaction current and thus scale up the overall Cl yield, multiple series stacks can
2
be connected in parallel (Supplementary Fig. 42b). This configuration leads to proportionally higher
current densities and gas production volumes.
Beyond these electrical configurations, further optimizations can be implemented to adapt the
system for industrial-scale deployment. For example, refining the electrode switching protocol and
optimizing Ag/AgCl electrode size (e.g., enlarge the electrode size, automating the periodic reversal
of Ag/AgCl electrodes to sustain Cl⁻ transport) can minimize downtime and enhance continuous
operation (Science 2024, 385, 1438-1444). Reducing reservoir volume and electrode spacing within
units could lower internal resistance and improve efficiency (International Journal of Hydrogen Energy
2003, 28, 35-41; Journal of Cleaner Production 2021, 319).
We have incorporated this discussion into the revised manuscript, including a reference to
Supplementary Fig. 42 for visual clarity, to better highlight the system's scalability potential. We
revised the Discussion section,
“The modular design of our system allows scalable applications by connecting multiple units in
series or parallel (Supplementary Fig. 42). Further improvements could be achieved by reducing
electrode spacing and automating the electrode switching.”

Q10: Generating Cl₂ in an open system raises safety concerns. While HER and CER are spatially
separated, the authors should discuss gas handling and containment strategies to support practical
implementation.
A10: Thank you very much for reminding us of this safety consideration! This problem is also
encountered by the conventional chlor-alkali process. The Cl₂ can be sealed to ensure safety. In our
system, the Cl₂ generation compartment can also be sealed, and we can maintain a negative pressure
within the sealed compartment. Sealed compartments would allow direct piping of Cl to storage or
2
processing units, while negative pressure (e.g., via vacuum-assisted collection) would prevent outward
leakage by drawing gases inward (J. Modern Chlor‐Alkali Technology 2001; Handbook of Chlor-
Alkali Technology 2005). These adaptations are compatible with our system's modular configuration.
Here, we revised the Discussion section in our manuscript to,
“...Regarding chlorine handling, we can seal the anode compartment and maintain slight negative
pressure to prevent chlorine leakage, ensuring both safety and directed transport to storage units.”
